## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a robot pass every trial and still lack the evidence needed for deployment?_

A robot that repeatedly opens one door has supplied evidence about that door, its own hardware, and the conditions of those trials. It has not established how it will behave at a displaced latch, with a different payload, or after its sensors drift, and a perfect record of a few dozen runs remains consistent with a policy that fails one attempt in ten. Its admitted actions also change the observations it receives, so agreement with recorded demonstrations cannot substitute for testing the resulting motion. Physical trials expose that feedback, but each consumes time and mechanical life, every further factor of ten in demonstrated reliability costs roughly ten times the trials, and protective interventions stop some trajectories before their consequences unfold. A team that reads a clean record as readiness releases the machine into conditions no trial visited and credits the learned policy with protection its supervisors supplied. Evaluation exists to prevent that error. It ties each task outcome to the conditions sampled, keeps every intervention in the record, states the uncertainty that remains, and names the uncovered conditions the rest of the machine must guard. Because actions cross an irreversible causal boundary, evidence of policy competence must remain distinct from permission to move.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Interpret physical success rates as conditional evidence about a specified machine, environment, and trial protocol
- Interpret completion and intervention metrics without crediting the policy for protection supplied by its supervision
- Compare open-loop prediction accuracy with closed-loop behavior shaped by the policy's own actions
- Select the evidence regime (replay, simulation, shadow operation, or constrained physical testing) that can answer a given evaluation question
- Design a predeclared trial protocol with fixed outcome rules and full-denominator accounting of interventions and aborts
- Calculate confidence bounds, trial counts, and test time for a zero-failure campaign under stated sampling assumptions
- Construct an evaluation record that bounds its operational claim and identifies coverage gaps and required protections
- Evaluate which rare failures remain unsupported by feasible testing and the available statistical assumptions
- Diagnose how hardware differences, environmental changes, and stopping rules alter the claim a campaign can support

:::

## From Clean Runs to Bounded Claims {#sec-evaluation-door-campaign}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DOOR CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: chapter opener, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the lease fallacy.
# │ Show: the evaluated campaign (latch task, base stopped) and the machine
# │       values the chapter quotes: approach speed, tripwire, latch limit, rack
# │       capacity, chunk inference target, chunk period, and chunk lease;
# │       plus the Part II funnel
# │       the completed record carries (ledger cells, supported cells,
# │       known absences, manifest omissions).
# │ How: registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle;
# │      the standoff and the ledger counts (from @sec-data and
# │      @sec-training) are chapter-local inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_frequency, check, MarkdownStr

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EvalMachine:
    """The latch campaign Ch7 evaluates, on the book's running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    standoff = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; base start distance from the door
    v_approach = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative; guarded approach, the declared ODD's speed
    f_latch_limit = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative; latch damage limit
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative; contact tripwire that ends an attempt (@sec-data)
    rack_capacity = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen; tote-rack capacity
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk policy rate
    t_chunk_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 of the ACT chunk policy incl. vision (M5)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease
    n_plate_positions = 3  # category: illustrative; nominal and two displaced plates, the scenario ledger of @sec-data
    ledger_speeds = [AISLE.v_latch_approach, AISLE.v_latch_high]  # category: illustrative; the ledger's two approach speeds
    n_supported = 1  # category: illustrative; the nominal plate at the guarded approach (LatchScenarioLedger in @sec-data)
    n_omissions = 2  # category: illustrative; soft penalty contact and missing transport lag, the manifest's omission log

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    n_speeds = len(ledger_speeds)
    n_cells = n_plate_positions * n_speeds
    n_absences = n_cells - n_supported

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_approach.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded approach is not 0.03 m/s")
    check(abs(f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit is not 100 N")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Contact tripwire is not 15 N")
    check(f_trip < f_latch_limit, "The tripwire must end an attempt well below the damage limit")
    check(abs(rack_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is not 50 kg")
    check(abs(chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk period is not 50 ms")
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is not 60 ms")
    check(chunk_period < t_lease, "Chunk period must fit inside the lease")
    check(abs(t_chunk_infer.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk inference target is not 40 ms")
    check(t_chunk_infer < chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(n_cells == 6 and n_supported == 1 and n_absences == 5, "Ledger should have one supported cell of six (matches @sec-data)")
    check(n_omissions == 2, "Manifest omission log holds two unclosed departures (matches @sec-training)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    standoff_str = fmt_length(standoff, precision=0)
    v_approach_str = fmt_velocity(v_approach, precision=2)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    rack_capacity_str = fmt_mass(rack_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period)
    t_chunk_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_infer)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease)
    _words = {1: "one", 2: "two", 3: "three", 5: "five", 6: "six"}
    n_plate_positions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_plate_positions])
    n_speeds_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_speeds])
    n_cells_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_cells])
    n_supported_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_supported])
    n_absences_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_absences])
    n_omissions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_omissions])
```

Evaluation turns observed behavior into a claim that other engineers can rely on. In static machine learning the procedure is settled: a held-out dataset is drawn once from a fixed distribution, the model scores each example independently, and the score describes the model on that distribution. A learned policy that moves a physical machine breaks each part of that procedure. Its admitted actions choose the states it later observes, so no fixed dataset can hold its test inputs. Each trial consumes test-cell time and mechanical life, so samples are small and expensive. A failed trial delivers energy across the causal boundary that cannot be recalled, so protective stops and human takeovers end some trials before their outcome is known, and the record holds observations that are neither successes nor failures. Aircraft, vehicle, and industrial-machine qualification face the last two problems for conventional controllers, whose behavior can be analyzed before test; a learned proposer adds the first, because its behavior can only be sampled.

The central question of this chapter is what a finite campaign of closed-loop trials can establish about a learned proposer, and what it must hand to the rest of the machine as unestablished. The answer has four parts. A success rate belongs to a declared population of machine, environment, and protocol, and it must be counted so that protection supplied by supervision is not credited to the policy (@sec-evaluation-what-measured). Only trials that close the loop through the permission path measure what the proposer does, and each evidence regime, from recorded replay to constrained physical testing, answers a different question (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics and @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes). A predeclared protocol turns a clean record into a one-sided confidence bound, and each further nine of demonstrated reliability costs ten times the trials (@sec-evaluation-trial-protocol, @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival, and @sec-evaluation-trial-limits). Finally, the evaluation record, the link of the record chain that follows the policy manifest, states the supported claim beside the conditions no trial visited, and those gaps, with the rare hazards no feasible campaign can bound, become obligations for runtime monitors and the permission path (@sec-evaluation-logs and @sec-evaluation-limits). The chapter closes with the procedural errors that let a campaign answer an easier question than its claim asks.

The running machine makes the question concrete. Fresh from the offline training pipeline, `latch-bc-01` is flashed onto the warehouse mobile manipulator; it is the checkpoint admitted by the original policy manifest in @sec-training-policy-manifest for this nominal campaign. In the illustrative initial validation campaign, suppose the machine completes twenty consecutive runs of its door task. Each run starts with the base `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide) from the spring-latched cage door; the base drives in and stops, and with the base at rest the arm unlatches and opens the door at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, without a contact-tripwire crossing or a human intervention. Its empirical sample success rate is $\hat{p} = 1.00$ (100 percent). On a static benchmark a perfect score would close the question. On the machine it leaves the deployment decision open, because twenty clean runs establish only a lower confidence limit and leave substantial uncertainty about failures the campaign did not observe.

The campaign needs an outcome rule and a sampled population before its perfect observed fraction can be interpreted. The same record must distinguish what the learned policy accomplished from what supervision supplied.

## Metric Coverage and Limitations of Scalar Success Rates {#sec-evaluation-what-measured}

The same latch policy can open the nominal door and jam against a displaced strike plate. Its measured success rate therefore belongs to the coupled policy, mechanical plant, computational hardware, environment, and trial protocol. Even a reproducible offline score describes a model on a specified dataset, not its behavior under arbitrary conditions.

To evaluate a policy, an engineering team executes a sequence of discrete physical runs. A single trial is fully determined only when every variable that can alter the physical state trajectory is fixed or explicitly sampled. Formally, let a single trial condition be defined by a tuple $c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa)$, drawn from an operational testing distribution $\mathcal{D}$. The vector $s_0$ represents the initial state of the machine: its pose (position and orientation), linear and angular velocities, and joint encoder positions. The environment vector $e$ captures external variables such as floor friction ($\mu$), ambient illuminance, obstacle geometry, and ambient air temperature. The machine state $m$ captures physical and hardware properties drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, encompassing unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances, battery state of charge, payload mass, tire wear, lost motion and compliance in the arm's transmissions\index{Mechanical backlash}, and sensor calibration matrices. The computational configuration $\pi_\theta$ encompasses the frozen policy weights $\theta$, inference quantization, scheduling deadlines, and software versions. Finally, the termination protocol $\kappa = (T_{\max}, g, \phi)$ defines the execution time limit $T_{\max}$, the spatial goal region $g$, and the binary evaluation function $\phi$ that maps the resulting trajectory to a terminal outcome $Y \in \{0, 1\}$.

In static machine learning benchmarks, inputs $(x_i, y_i)$ are sampled independently from a static data distribution $p_{\text{data}}(x, y)$. In Physical AI, the continuous trajectory $\text{Traj}(c) = (s_0, u_0, s_1, u_1, \dots, s_T)$ is generated sequentially by the closed-loop physical state transition kernel:
$$s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{T}(s_t, u_t; m, e), \quad a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t), \quad u_t = \text{Gate}(a_t, s_t)$$
The true success probability under this evaluation protocol is the expected value of the binary task outcome averaged over the joint distribution of trial conditions:
$$p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$$ {#eq-eval-estimand}
Here $\text{Traj}(c)$ is the physical trajectory generated under condition $c$. Changing floor friction or battery voltage changes the transition kernel $\mathcal{T}$ even with identical weights $\theta$. The sampling protocol is consequently part of the quantity being estimated. @Sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution gives the formal integral.

In test engineering, the abstract distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is operationalized through a **stratified test matrix**[^fn-design-experiments-blocking] across controllable parameters, systematically varying payload mass, approach speed, illumination, and initial spatial standoff, while logging uncontrollable environmental parameters such as ambient temperature and floor friction. Unstratified, naive random sampling is inadequate because it oversamples benign nominal states while leaving boundary regions unvisited.

[^fn-design-experiments-blocking]: **Design of Experiments**\index{Design of experiments!stratified test matrix}: Fisher's agricultural field trials introduced randomization and blocking so that variation in the soil could not masquerade as a treatment effect [@fisher1935design]. A stratified test matrix blocks on payload, approach speed, and lighting for the same reason, and randomizing the run order keeps winding heat and spring relaxation from entering the comparison as if they were properties of the policy (@sec-evaluation-policy-comparison).

::: {#dfn-evaluation-closed-loop-estimand .callout-definition title="Closed-loop evaluation estimand"}

***Closed-loop evaluation estimand***\index{Closed-loop evaluation estimand!definition}\index{Evaluation estimand!definition} is the expected physical task outcome $p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$ defined over the joint distribution of initial states, mechanical plant wear, environmental physics, frozen policy weights, and evaluation predicates:
$$c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa) \sim \mathcal{D}$$
rather than an intrinsic property of the neural policy weights evaluated in isolation.

1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is treated as a property of the model $\pi_\theta$. In physical AI, substituting a worn tire, letting battery voltage sag, or shifting ambient illuminance alters the physical state transition function without changing a single weight. The sampling distribution of operational conditions $\mathcal{D}$ is an inseparable part of the quantity being estimated.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike open-loop validation metrics (such as validation loss, cosine similarity, or mean squared trajectory error) which score predictions against frozen recorded states, the closed-loop estimand integrates over the endogenous feedback loop where past actions physically move the machine, directly changing the future sensor observations it will receive.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reporting a single success rate percentage without predeclaring the support, density, and environmental bounds of the test distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Any physical policy can be made arbitrarily successful by testing exclusively in benign, unperturbed states.

:::

### Hardware instance variance and environmental unobservables

The physical mechanisms that alter $c$ between trials operate independently of the policy, and the mobile manipulator exhibits each of them across two major sources of dispersion: **hardware instance variance** and **environmental unobservables**.

First, hardware instance variance reflects the physical reality that robotic production lines do not manufacture identical copies. Even within the same manufacturing batch, robots exhibit unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances:

- **Transmission lost motion and compliance**: The arm's strain-wave (harmonic) drives have no backlash at the gear mesh by design; their dominant nonlinearities are torsional compliance and hysteresis, and couplings or planetary stages elsewhere in a drivetrain add true backlash [@harmonicdrive2006csf]. These properties differ from unit to unit and grow with wear. Under direction reversals they introduce nonlinear hysteresis and phase lag that can destabilize tight neural feedback loops, so each unit's lost motion and stiffness are measured on the bench rather than taken from a nominal.
- **Structural link compliance**: Elastic link deflection under payload varies across chassis assemblies, shifting the true Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool center point} relative to forward kinematics calculations.
- **Sensor assembly misalignments**: Real camera mounts and depth sensor brackets deviate from their CAD nominals, introducing systematic coordinate frame offsets between sensor frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{cam}}$ and base frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{base}}$ whose size an extrinsic calibration of each unit measures.
- **Actuator electrical variance**: Motor phase resistances and torque constants ($K_t$) differ across stator windings by amounts the drive datasheet's tolerance or a per-unit characterization states. Furthermore, as the battery discharges\index{State of charge (SoC)}, the drives lose voltage headroom against back-electromotive force (back-EMF)\index{Back-EMF}, shifting the torque-speed curve\index{Torque-speed curve} and diminishing acceleration authority.

Second, environmental unobservables alter the physical interaction dynamics without changing camera pixels in a way the neural network recognizes. Ambient daylight shifting across the warehouse alters illuminance, causing camera auto-exposure to stretch shutter times, inducing motion blur during base turns. Direct solar glare at dawn or dusk saturates complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor arrays, washing out visual contrast at the latch interface. On the floor, dust accumulation and ambient humidity alter the tire-floor friction coefficient ($\mu$), extending braking distance. In the manipulator arm, repeated door openings generate Joule heating ($I^2 R$)\index{Joule heating} in motor windings and warm harmonic drive lubricants, decreasing damping and expanding link dimensions. Consequently, the tool-center point meets the latch at a different spatial offset on a hot afternoon than on a cold morning. A policy evaluated across twenty trials on Unit 01 in the morning may fail completely when tested on Unit 02 in the afternoon, despite running identical frozen weights.

The reset procedure moves $c$ as well. An operator who repositions the base after a difficult run may favor an easy start, and an automated reset that repeats one path heats the windings cyclically. An operator who catches a failing run and discards it as a reset erases the hardest failure from the sample. Statistical evaluation must therefore distinguish sampling variation from a change in the estimand. When $n$ trials are drawn from a fixed $\mathcal{D}$, the sample proportion $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$ fluctuates around $p(\mathcal{D})$, and standard estimators bound that noise. Loading the tote rack or moving the door's strike plate changes the experiment to a different distribution $\mathcal{D}'$ with its own $p(\mathcal{D}')$, and pooling the two samples combines observations from two different machines.

### Intervention-based physical metrics

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-jam-reset
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESET SHARE OF A JAMMED DOOR RUN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Reset Latency item in @sec-evaluation-what-measured.
# │ Show: the share of test-cell occupancy a jammed-latch reset consumes.
# │ How: share = t_jam_reset / (t_run + t_jam_reset); t_run matches DoorCycle.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time, fmt_percent, check

class JamReset:
    """Occupancy share of a manual reset after a jammed latch."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_run = 25.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; door run, same as DoorCycle.t_run
    t_jam_reset = 60.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; clear a jammed pin, recalibrate, return to standoff

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reset_share = (t_jam_reset / (t_run + t_jam_reset)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.70 < reset_share < 0.72, "Jammed-latch reset should take about 71 percent of occupancy")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_run_str = fmt_time(t_run, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_jam_reset_str = fmt_time(t_jam_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    reset_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(reset_share, precision=1)
```

A door may open after the permission path slightly reduces the proposed force. That run can satisfy the whole-machine service requirement while exposing a limitation of the raw proposer. A stop short of the door can instead preserve the physical limit while failing the task. A human recovery can complete the task without demonstrating unassisted autonomy. These outcomes require separate fields.

We therefore report whole-machine task completion within its time and physical limits, raw proposer autonomy, and protective outcomes independently. Normal least-change adjustments remain part of the designed machine. They reduce the strict unassisted metric below, but do not automatically make a completed task a system failure. Intervention logs distinguish adjustments, rejected proposals, protective stops, and human takeovers, with a predeclared event-counting rule so a sustained clamp is not confused with many independent incidents.

1. **Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR)**\index{Autonomous Completion Rate!definition}: Let $I_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ be the total count of supervisory interventions (whether by human operators, runtime permission filters, or emergency tripwires) during trial $i$, and let $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote goal achievement within the time limit $T_{\max}$. The unassisted autonomous success indicator is defined as:
   $$A_i = \mathbb{I}(Y_i = 1 \land I_i = 0)$$
   The Autonomous Completion Rate is the sample proportion of completely unassisted trials:
   $$\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n A_i = \frac{N_{\text{unassisted}}}{n}$$
   ACR here measures strict raw proposer autonomy: even one recorded override gives $A_i = 0$. The separate task outcome $Y_i$ may still be one when normal filtering permits completion within the declared service limits.

2. **Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**\index{Mean Time Between Interventions!definition}: For a declared intervention class, MTBI measures its frequency during active execution:
   $$T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{T_{\text{active}}}{N_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n I_i}$$
   where $t_{\text{active}, i}$ is the active operating duration of trial $i$ and $N_{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i$ is the total number of recorded interventions. MTBI measures the burden of that event class. Frequent automatic adjustments and frequent human takeovers have different staffing consequences; neither this ratio nor zero observed damage establishes deployment readiness.

3. **Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$)**\index{Intervention Density!definition}: In spatial navigation and continuous trajectory tracking, interventions must be normalized against physical exposure distance or discrete control steps:
   $$D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n L_i} \quad [\text{interventions per kilometer}] \quad \text{or} \quad D_{\text{int}} = 1{,}000 \times \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_{\text{steps}, i}} \quad [\text{interventions per } 1{,}000 \text{ steps}]$$
   where $L_i$ is the path distance traversed. Intervention density exposes whether policy degradation is uniformly distributed or concentrated at specific geometric bottlenecks (such as narrow doorway passages).

4. **Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)**\index{Reset Latency!definition}: In physical qualification campaigns, the true experimental cost is governed by the time required to recover the plant and environment after a trial concludes or aborts:
   $$T_{\text{reset}} = t_{\text{physical\_restore}} + t_{\text{calibration}} + t_{\text{telemetry\_flush}}$$
   The door run takes `{python} JamReset.t_run_str` of active execution. Its nominal reset is short (@sec-evaluation-trial-costs), but a run that jams the latch needs a manual reset of about `{python} JamReset.t_jam_reset_str` (illustrative) to clear the pin, recalibrate joint encoders, and return the base to its standoff. For such runs the reset consumes `{python} JamReset.reset_share_pct_str` percent of test-cell occupancy. Campaigns with high reset latency create intense organizational pressure to take shortcuts, such as skipping motor thermal cooldown or repositioning the robot to easier initial poses, and each shortcut corrupts trial stationarity.

MTBI is not a Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF). An MTBF counts a separately defined failure event, which need not be destruction, whereas MTBI, ACR, and $D_{\text{int}}$ describe intervention burden and strict proposer autonomy inside the tested envelope. Zero hardware damage can therefore coexist with frequent takeovers or automatic adjustments, and counting a run that supervision cut short as unassisted survival commits the censored trial fallacy (@sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes).

The outcome definitions identify what to count. The next choice is how to expose the feedback that can change those outcomes.

## Closed-Loop Dynamics {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics}

In standard deep learning pipelines, model performance is evaluated by computing empirical risk across a static held-out validation split $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)$$
Whether the target metric is Top-1 classification accuracy, token perplexity, F1 score, or action regression loss, evaluation is fundamentally passive and decoupled. The data-generating process is feedforward and memoryless with respect to the model's predictions: mispredicting sample $i$ has zero causal influence on sample $i+1$ ($\partial x_{i+1} / \partial \hat{y}_i = 0$).

Carrying this paradigm over to a physical policy produces the **offline evaluation illusion**, the mistaken belief that lower validation loss, higher action cosine similarity, or smaller Mean Squared Error (MSE) on logged data establishes superior physical performance. Such loss functions $\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \|a_i^* - \pi_\theta(s_i^*)\|^2$ score predictions along frozen demonstrator trajectories. The illusion is measured, not hypothetical. In a controlled study of imitation learning on simulated and real manipulation tasks, the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss was consistently worse in rollouts than the best checkpoint, and rollout success could rise while validation loss rose [@mandlekar2021matters].

The decoupling that validates offline scoring vanishes in Physical AI. Actions cross the causal boundary into mass, momentum, and non-smooth contact mechanics. The policy's admitted actions physically move the plant, endogenously creating subsequent sensory inputs ($s_{t+1} = f(s_t, u_t)$). Actions are not classifications; they are physical forces, torques, and velocity setpoints that interact with inertia, friction, and backlash. A navigation policy can reproduce recorded aisle runs almost perfectly under static regression metrics, yet spend the base's entire clearance to a storage rack before traversing a third of the aisle. The difference lies in what each kind of test feeds back to the policy.

In an **open-loop evaluation**\index{Open-loop evaluation!definition}, a candidate policy $\pi_\theta$ is scored across a static dataset of recorded demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} = \{(s_t^*, a_t^*)\}_{t=1}^T$. At each discrete timestep $t$, the policy receives a recorded demonstrator state $s_t^*$ and outputs a predicted action $\hat{a}_t = \pi_\theta(s_t^*)$. An error metric, such as mean squared error or cross-entropy, measures the distance between $\hat{a}_t$ and the recorded expert action $a_t^*$. At step $t+1$, the evaluation pipeline supplies the next recorded state $s_{t+1}^*$ from the dataset. The action $\hat{a}_t$ produced by the policy is discarded without executing on hardware, keeping the sequence of input states independent of the policy's past outputs ($\partial s_{t+1}^* / \partial \hat{a}_t = 0$). In a **closed-loop evaluation**\index{Closed-loop evaluation!definition}, the policy proposes $a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t)$; the permission path checks it against measured state and constraints, applies $u_t$ (or a fallback), and the plant evolves as $s_{t+1} = f(s_t,u_t)$. The applied command changes the physical state and later observations, crossing the causal boundary in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}
*Admitted actions choose the next observation.*
:::

### Compounding error and kinematic integration {#sec-evaluation-compounding-error}

A neural policy with negligible open-loop validation loss can still drive a physical robot off course within seconds. Open-loop evaluation tests actions only along the demonstrator's state trajectory, where inputs are reset to expert states at every clock cycle. In closed-loop deployment, the policy's own admitted actions move the plant, so small prediction errors perturb the observations that follow.

The gap has a worst-case form, derived in @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability. If the policy disagrees with the expert with probability at most $\epsilon$ per step on recorded expert states, open-loop scoring over $T$ steps accumulates at most $T\epsilon$ disagreements, whereas in closed loop a single early disagreement can leave the policy in unscored states for the rest of the horizon, and the imitation cost can grow as $T^2\epsilon$ (@eq-data-quadratic-drift). For evaluation, the consequence is that an open-loop score understates closed-loop cost by up to a factor of the horizon. The bound concerns zero-one disagreement cost and does not apply directly to unbounded MSE, contact force, or damage severity. A separate kinematic calculation shows one physical consequence of persistent error: an uncorrected heading or steering bias integrates forward into macroscopic lateral displacement, causing the robot to exhaust its safe clearance envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEADING BIAS AGAINST THE AISLE'S SIDE CLEARANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Show: where a persistent 1 degree heading bias of the navigation stack
# │       (not the evaluated latch policy) spends the aisle's side clearance.
# │ How: y(t) = v sin(eps) t; t_impact = W_clear / (v sin(eps)); the side
# │      clearance is (aisle width - machine width) / 2.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_angle, fmt_math, sci_latex, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class AisleDrift:
    """Closed-loop drift of a biased navigation policy on the running machine's aisle."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative; side clearance each side
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    machine_width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative; base footprint
    heading_offset_deg = 1.0  # category: illustrative; persistent heading bias

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = math.radians(heading_offset_deg)
    eps_q = eps * radian
    angular_mse = (eps_q**2).to(radian**2)  # open-loop score on recorded centerline states
    t_impact = (clearance / (v * math.sin(eps))).to(ureg.second)
    x_impact = (v * t_impact).to(ureg.meter)
    aisle_fraction = (x_impact / aisle_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Side clearance is not 0.15 m")
    check(abs(((aisle_width - machine_width) / 2 - clearance).to(ureg.meter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Side clearance must equal (aisle - machine) / 2")
    check(abs(aisle_length.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, "Aisle length is not 30 m")
    check(abs(x_impact.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 8.6) < 0.05, "Clearance should be spent in about 8.6 m")
    check(abs(t_impact.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 5.73) < 0.005, "Clearance should be spent in about 5.7 s")
    check(aisle_fraction < 1 / 3, "Prose says less than a third of the aisle")
    check(abs(heading_offset_deg - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Prose, fig-cap, and fig-alt state a 1.0 degree heading offset")
    check(abs(angular_mse.magnitude - 3.05e-4) < 5e-7, "fig-alt states an angular MSE of 3.05e-4 rad^2")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, precision=2)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, precision=0)
    machine_width_str = fmt_length(machine_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    clearance_cm_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    t_impact_str = fmt_time(t_impact, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    x_impact_str = fmt_length(x_impact, precision=1)
    eps_rad_str = fmt_angle(eps_q, precision=5)
    angular_mse_math = fmt_math(rf"{sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
    angular_mse_eq = fmt_math(rf"\text{{MSE}}_\theta = ({fmt(eps, precision=5)})^2 \approx {sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
```

A policy whose own actions carry it off the states it was trained on is the endogenous-data principle at work (\ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}); @sec-data-endogenous-experience developed its consequence for data, and evaluation must measure it on the machine. The door campaign cannot show the effect, because its base stands still while the arm works, so the example comes from the same machine's navigation stack rather than from the latch policy under evaluation. The base drives a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle at its `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit (both illustrative), and the nominal expert demonstration follows the centerline with heading $\theta^* = 0\text{ rad}$ and lateral offset $y^* = 0\text{ m}$. Suppose the candidate navigation policy has a systematic heading bias of $\epsilon_\theta = 1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) on every step, and the permission path admits each of these proposals because none is infeasible on its own while clearance remains.

In an open-loop evaluation, the policy receives the demonstrator state $s_t^* = (x_t^*, 0, 0)$ at each step and predicts a forward velocity with a $1.0^\circ$ steering offset. The offline scoring pipeline records a mean absolute angular error of $1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) and an extremely low mean squared error of `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_eq`.[^fn-math-openloop-mse] In closed-loop execution, however, because the machine physically moves based on previously admitted commands, uncorrected heading errors compound continuously over time. Under planar unicycle kinematics[^fn-unicycle-model-drift] ($\dot{y} = v \sin \theta \approx v \epsilon_\theta$), a persistent angular offset integrates into a cumulative lateral displacement:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin \epsilon_\theta \, d\tau \approx v \epsilon_\theta t$$
If the policy exhibits a persistent yaw-rate bias $\omega_{\text{bias}}$ (steering drift) rather than a fixed heading offset, the heading angle itself grows linearly over time ($\theta(t) = \int_0^t \omega_{\text{bias}} \, d\tau = \omega_{\text{bias}} t$). Integrating forward velocity $v$ then produces a cumulative lateral excursion that compounds quadratically in time:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin(\omega_{\text{bias}} \tau) \, d\tau \approx \frac{1}{2} v \omega_{\text{bias}} t^2$$
Quadratic kinematic drift and the worst-case imitation-cost bound describe different quantities. The first integrates a persistent yaw-rate bias; the second bounds accumulated decision cost under distribution shift. Neither establishes exponential instability.

For the constant $1.0^\circ$ heading bias, the base is `{python} AisleDrift.machine_width_str` wide in a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_width_str` aisle, which leaves $W_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str` of side clearance to the rack on each side, and the drift spends that clearance at
$$t_{\text{impact}} = \frac{W_{\text{clear}}}{v \sin \epsilon_\theta},$$ {#eq-eval-clearance-time}
which at the drive limit is `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str`, after `{python} AisleDrift.x_impact_str` of travel and less than a third of the way down the aisle (@fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop). Either the permission path's clearance check stops the base short of the rack or, without that check, the base strikes it. Both outcomes are a failed trial that open-loop scoring rated near-perfect.

[^fn-math-openloop-mse]: **Mean Masking of Steering Spikes**\index{Evaluation!metric masking}: Averaging squared steering error over thousands of straight-aisle frames also hides a brief, large prediction spike, which barely moves the mean. Whether such a spike matters depends on whether its integrated motion spends the clearance before the permission path responds, a question only a plant and timing model can answer.

[^fn-unicycle-model-drift]: **Unicycle Model**\index{Unicycle model!lateral drift}: The simplest planar vehicle model, in which pose $(x, y, \theta)$ evolves as $\dot x = v\cos\theta$, $\dot y = v\sin\theta$, $\dot\theta = \omega$. It keeps the constraint that matters for the aisle. A wheeled base cannot move sideways, so any heading error becomes travel toward the rack.

The aisle example shows both reasons that an open-loop score\index{Open-loop evaluation!closed-loop gap} decouples from closed-loop survival. First, static evaluation cannot integrate a persistent error into displacement. It resets the machine to an expert state at every clock cycle, masking the compounding of integration errors, whereas in closed loop the state at index $t$ is the expanded composition of all previous actions:
$$s_t = f(f(\dots f(s_0, u_0)\dots, u_{t-2}), u_{t-1})$$
A persistent heading bias needs no software bug, since differential tire wear, camera-mast vibration, or floor camber produces one. Second, static evaluation cannot follow the machine into the unfamiliar states that early errors steer it toward. The first admitted error moves the base from the demonstrated state $s_1^*$ to an unvisited state $s_1$, and once it drifts a few centimeters off the centerline it occupies states absent from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}$. The offline metric, computed only where $y = 0\text{ m}$, holds no evidence about $\pi_\theta(s)$ for $y \neq 0\text{ m}$, and a policy never shown recoveries from off-center states can make larger errors there, accelerating the divergence that @sec-training-synthesis-regimes traced for behavioral cloning.

<!-- fig-alt below hand-types values because fig-alt cannot hold inline python. Keep them in sync with these cell outputs:
     "one-degree heading offset"          = AisleDrift.heading_offset_deg (1.0)
     "3.05 times 10 to the minus four"    = AisleDrift.angular_mse_math (the fig-cap and prose use it inline)
     "1.5 meters per second"              = AisleDrift.v_str (RM.base.max_velocity, the drive limit)
     "15-centimeter side clearance"       = AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str
     "about 5.7 seconds"                  = AisleDrift.t_impact_str
     "8.6 meters along the aisle"         = AisleDrift.x_impact_str
     Guards in calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift pin 1.0 degree, 3.05e-4 rad^2, 1.5 m/s, 0.15 m, 5.7 s, and 8.6 m.

::: {#fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open vs. closed loop divergence**: A persistent $1.0^\circ$ heading offset gives `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_math` angular mean squared error on recorded centerline states. On the mobile manipulator's aisle, the navigation stack's admitted motion with that fixed heading drifts linearly and reaches the `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_str` side clearance after `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str` at the `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit. The example concerns the navigation stack, not the latch policy under evaluation." fig-alt="Two-panel aisle example. Left: recorded-state replay scores a constant one-degree heading offset with angular mean squared error 3.05 times 10 to the minus four radians squared and resets the next input to the recorded centerline. Right: if that heading persists in a physical rollout at 1.5 meters per second, lateral drift grows linearly and reaches the 15-centimeter side clearance after about 5.7 seconds, 8.6 meters along the aisle. Policy proposals pass through the permission path before the plant moves."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPEN-LOOP REPLAY VS. CLOSED-LOOP DRIFT (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop
# │ Goal:    show why a heading error that is invisible offline spends clearance
# │ Show:    lateral offset against forward position, replay beside physical loop
# │ How:     one heading offset drives both panels and both numbers;
# │          speed and clearance come from the aisle via calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

COLORS = viz.COLORS

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario parameters) ────────────────────────────────────────────
HEADING_OFFSET_DEG = AisleDrift.heading_offset_deg  # category: illustrative; from the LEGO cell
CLEARANCE_M = AisleDrift.clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative; AISLE.side_clearance
SPEED_MS = AisleDrift.v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude  # category: illustrative; RM.base.max_velocity (drive limit)
REACH_M = 10.0  # category: chosen; plot extent, the first third of the aisle

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theta = math.radians(HEADING_OFFSET_DEG)
angular_mse = theta**2  # rad^2, the offline error signal
exhausted_m = CLEARANCE_M / math.tan(theta)  # where the drift reaches clearance
exhausted_s = exhausted_m / SPEED_MS

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, (ax_a, ax_b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), sharey=True)
x = np.linspace(0, REACH_M, 400)

ax_a.plot(x, np.zeros_like(x), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_a.plot(np.arange(0, REACH_M, 2), np.zeros(int(REACH_M // 2)), "o", ms=5, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])
ax_a.text(
    0.6,
    0.107,
    "Each next input returns to\nthe recorded centerline",
    fontsize=9,
    va="center",
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="white", ec=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.0),
)
ax_a.text(0.6, 0.030, f"Angular MSE: {angular_mse:.2e} rad$^2$".replace("e-04", r" $\times$ 10$^{-4}$"), fontsize=9, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])

ax_b.plot(x, x * math.tan(theta), color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_b.axhline(0.0, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax_b.axvline(exhausted_m, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 2)))
ax_b.plot([exhausted_m], [CLEARANCE_M], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["RedLine"], zorder=5)
ax_b.text(
    exhausted_m - 0.35, CLEARANCE_M - 0.075, f"Clearance exhausted\nat {exhausted_s:.1f} s", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha="right", va="top"
)
ax_b.text(0.6, 0.182, f"y = x tan({HEADING_OFFSET_DEG:.0f}°) under fixed heading", fontsize=9)

for ax, title, lx, lha in ((ax_a, "(a) Recorded-state replay", REACH_M - 0.15, "right"), (ax_b, "(b) Physical closed loop", 0.6, "left")):
    ax.axhline(CLEARANCE_M, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.2, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
    ax.text(lx, CLEARANCE_M + 0.006, f"{CLEARANCE_M * 100:.0f} cm clearance", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha=lha, va="bottom")
    ax.set_xlim(0, REACH_M)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 0.225)
    ax.set_xticks(range(0, int(REACH_M) + 1, 2))
    ax.set_xlabel("Forward position (m)")
    ax.text(0.0, 1.02, title, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

ax_a.set_yticks([0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20])
ax_a.set_ylabel("Lateral offset (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
