The peak force is then
$$F_{\text{peak}} = k_{\text{contact}} x_{\text{max}} = v_{\text{approach}} \sqrt{m_{\text{red}}\, k_{\text{contact}}}$$
reached after a quarter period, $\Delta t_{\text{rise}} \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{m_{\text{red}} / k_{\text{contact}}}$, in this undamped idealization. Requiring the peak to stay below a force limit $F_{\text{limit}}$ gives the admissible approach speed
$$v_{\text{approach}} \le \frac{F_{\text{limit}}}{\sqrt{m_{\text{red}}\, k_{\text{contact}}}},$$ {#eq-eval-impact-speed}
the same transient-contact relation that ISO/TS 15066 Annex A uses to set maximum relative speeds for power- and force-limited collaborative robots [@isots15066]. ISO 10218-2:2025 incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066; ISO/TS 15066:2016 itself remains published and is under revision, with a successor, ISO 15066-1, in development [@iso10218part2]. Evaluating the bound on the latch needs the arm's effective mass at the gripper and the latch's contact stiffness, both of which must be measured for the configuration; neither is in the machine's data sheet. The evaluation consequence does not depend on those values. A monitor whose detection and physical response take longer than the rise time cannot reduce the first peak, however fast the neural inference, so the campaign measures force-time traces at the load path and validates the two protections that act before contact: passive compliance, which lowers $k_{\text{contact}}$ and stretches the rise time, and a precontact speed limit such as the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach. Extreme value theory (EVT)\index{Extreme value theory} offers candidate models for maxima, but a Gumbel, Fréchet, or Weibull family must be fitted to a defined sample of block maxima or threshold exceedances, checked against alternatives, and reported with its uncertainty; the physical mechanism alone does not select the family.[^fn-math-extreme-value] Without those data, @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails states what to measure and what protection to validate rather than predicting rare-event frequencies.

[^fn-math-extreme-value]: **Extreme Value Theory**\index{Extreme value theory!origins}: @fisher1928limiting found the three limiting forms that the largest member of a large sample can take, @gnedenko1943distribution proved that under general conditions no other limits exist, and @gumbel1958statistics made the theory an engineering tool for floods and material fatigue. Each of those applications fitted many block maxima. The latch campaign yields one maximum per run, twenty in all, too few to choose a family, let alone fit one.

| Disturbance channel     | Peak quantity and sampling record                    | Physical consequence to test                             | Candidate protection to validate                                                  |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Compute and bus latency | Per-cycle end-to-end age and deadline misses         | Stale proposals erode braking margin                     | Freshness lease and independently timed fallback                                  |
| Contact shock           | Force-time trace, impulse, and peak at the load path | Yield or overload before a reactive command takes effect | Passive compliance and precontact speed limit; reactive limits address later load |
| Low traction            | Local friction estimate and stopping response        | Slip extends stopping distance                           | Conservative speed ceiling and tested fallback on low-grip surfaces               |
| Optical glare           | Saturation duration and perception misses            | False clearance or lost state estimate                   | Redundant sensing and independent physical constraints                            |

: **Peak-disturbance evidence and protection**: Mechanisms identify measurements and safeguards, not an EVT family or event rate. Any quantitative tail claim needs a defined population, fitted model, goodness-of-fit checks, and uncertainty. {#tbl-07-extreme-value-tails tbl-colwidths="[18,28,26,28]"}

The latch shows why the contact-shock row pairs a measurement with a protection. Each door run contributes one block maximum, its peak latch force, and twenty maxima are far too few to fit a tail that would predict how often a run crosses `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str`. A force monitor that reacts only after contact cannot undo the first peak either; its measured detection and actuator response can limit the loading that follows, while the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, a precontact speed limit, reserves the margin for the initial impact.

Distributing trials across a fleet does not buy independence. Ten machines tested concurrently in one warehouse share a production batch, a floor finish, a ventilation system, and operators trained under one protocol, so an anomaly absent from the facility, such as floor glazing or low-angle glare, reaches none of them. Ten thousand fleet hours in one facility are ten parallel observations of one narrow distribution, not ten thousand hours of independent exposure. Standardized test fixtures such as those in @fig-07-nist-test-arena buy repeatability by bounding the state space to the fixture.

::: {#fig-07-nist-test-arena fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Standardized robotic evaluation facility**: NIST response-robot test bays photographed in 2013 (Linda Joy/NIST); their test methods are standardized by ASTM subcommittee E54.09 on response robots. A zero-failure run across standardized bays establishes competence inside the arena and says nothing about glare, surface contaminants, or obstacles outside it." fig-alt="Photograph by Linda Joy/NIST of NIST response-robot test facility bays in 2013. Structured test spaces support repeatable trials within their fixture conditions."}
![](images/jpg/fig07_real_nist_test_arena.jpg){width="75%"}
:::

The repeatable challenges in @fig-07-nist-test-arena support comparisons across robotic platforms. Their controlled geometry, surfaces, and lighting also define the evidence boundary; testing factory spills, pedestrian crossings, or low-angle sunlight requires additional conditions in the campaign.

These ceilings force an architectural conclusion. Physical AI safety cannot rest on statistical confidence in the learned weights. The exposure examples at $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-9}$ failures per hour show why more trials cannot carry the whole protection argument. Runtime constraints must have their own evidence, including the assumptions under which they can prevent a hazardous action and the time available to respond. Policy trials characterize task completion and intervention rates within the tested envelope; they do not establish that the envelope will contain every fault. The protection argument therefore shifts toward the independent permission path and physical safeguards, whose limits require separate validation.

A model-based stability certificate, such as the Lyapunov argument of @sec-appendix-control-lyapunov\index{Lyapunov function!stability certification}, is a different kind of evidence from finite task trials, and the evaluated proposer supplies none. The machine therefore needs its own containment and fault evidence:

1. **Runtime Containment**: Bounding the physical authority of the learned policy by delegating the collaborative-robot force limits, kinematic acceleration limits, and emergency stops to the permission path, an independent, deterministic mechanism below the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. The protection claim then rests on the permission path and its fallback, whose state estimates, plant and actuator models, response timing, and reserved stopping margin must be validated separately from the policy.
2. **Fault Injection on Physical Benches**: Rather than waiting for passive disturbances to strike, engineers inject them. Injected trials follow the fault-injection method of @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list; their fault population belongs in a separate labeled ledger rather than being pooled with operational draws.

::: {#chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf .callout-checkpoint title="Sample size and MTBF evidence target"}

Before moving on, check your understanding of sample size scaling and physical test limits:

- [ ] **Exposure-wall estimate**: Under a stationary Poisson failure model, can you estimate the failure-free hours a relaxed `{python} MtbfCampaign.mtbf_relaxed_str` MTBF target needs at 95 percent confidence, and decide whether one rig running continuously for a year could supply them?
- [ ] **Mechanical fatigue exhaustion**: Can you explain why a campaign's wheel revolutions cannot be compared with a bearing $L_{10}$ rating without knowing the load the bearing carries?
- [ ] **Architectural containment vs. statistical sampling**: Can you explain why a task campaign needs separate evidence for runtime constraints and physical safeguards?

:::

Even under rigorous qualification protocols and automated test cells, statistical sampling alone cannot establish ultra-reliable autonomy. What remains outside any finite campaign, and which runtime monitors the record must name for it, decides how far the evidence can carry the release decision.

### Turning coverage gaps into runtime obligations

The limits of evaluation follow from the endogenous loop of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics. The states a physical campaign visits depend on the commands the permission path admitted, so no fixed dataset matches the candidate's closed-loop state distribution, and a simulator substitutes its own transition model for the plant's (formal trajectory distributions in @sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution). A simulator that models the aisle floor with the friction of clean, inspected concrete cannot show what the base does on a clear oil film, and one whose actuators respond instantly cannot show the lag of a real stator's electrical time constant\index{Actuator!stator delay}; the physical trajectory departs from the simulated one, and the departures compound into states no simulated run visited. A physical test therefore bounds only the distribution it actually sampled.

The door campaign's conclusion is correspondingly narrow. It establishes that one software build on one specific hardware unit (Unit 01), from the sampled initial conditions and inside the environmental lighting and temperature present during the runs, failed with probability below `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent at 95 percent confidence. It says nothing about a colder morning that derates the joints\index{Hardware!thermal derating}, a gearbox whose compliance\index{Hardware!gearbox compliance} and backlash have grown with wear, or a displaced strike plate.

A campaign that samples several units can support a broader declared population, but more runs on the nominal plate on Unit 01 only tighten the binomial bound (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds). Two thousand further runs would measure that single unit with finer precision while leaving the displaced-plate cells, the loaded machine, fleet-wide unit differences, and bus jitter\index{Hardware!bus jitter} exactly as unsupported as before.

Since evaluation cannot establish how the policy behaves outside the sampled distribution, each monitorable boundary of the claim needs a runtime signal, threshold, and tested response, and the permission path must enforce independent physical constraints. Distribution support is only partially observable and an OOD detector has measurable false negatives, so conditions that cannot be sensed reliably require ODD restrictions, passive protection, or other independent barriers. The evaluation record carries these specifications in its `runtime_monitor_specs` field (@sec-evaluation-logs). The field names five monitoring channels whose coverage and response must be measured:

1. **Input Support / Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!OOD detection} Estimates whether incoming observations depart from the tested distribution using a calibrated score and reports false negatives on held-out shifted conditions.
2. **Execution Latency Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!execution latency} Measures observation age and inference duration against their separate declared limits, checks proposal renewal against the expected cadence (for example, the latch policy's `{python} EvalMachine.t_chunk_infer_str` P99 inference target inside its `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period at `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str`), records misses, and checks that lease expiry invokes the validated fallback. A $P_{99}$ summary alone is not a hard deadline bound.
3. **Constraint Margin Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!constraint margin} Tracks the distance between the current physical state and hardware safety limits, including joint torque limits\index{Actuator!torque limit}, motor winding temperature\index{Actuator!Joule heating}, and obstacle clearance against limits specified for the hardware and stopping model.
4. **Intervention Rate Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!intervention rate} Calculates the frequency of permission-path overrides, detecting when policy instability causes excessive corrections.
5. **Environmental Assumption Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!environmental assumptions} Measures external operating conditions, such as surface traction estimated from wheel slip and ambient illumination measured by photometric sensors.

A monitor that only writes an anomaly to a log protects nothing. An invalid replacement is refused without automatically revoking a still-valid active command. When the active command's own state, evidence, or lease no longer permits continuation, the permission path acts on the actuators through a validated fallback, a speed restriction or a controlled stop, provided the sensed state, actuator capability, and reserved clearance make that response feasible (fallback logic in @sec-appendix-control-cbf). A timely, confident proposal still passes the independent state, clearance, and actuator checks before any $u_t$ is applied.

Some failures no software runtime monitor detects. This limitation constitutes the **epistemic trap of software OOD monitors**: an out-of-distribution detector operates entirely on digital sensor streams and latent representations. However, an optical illusion or sensor physics failure, such as a spotless clear glass partition, specular laser glare, or lens mud, can leave the perception model reporting familiar features while missing a physical obstacle. The software cannot detect what physical transduction failed to capture. A proposal can meet every deadline, respect every torque limit, and arise from apparently familiar latent features, yet steer the base directly into the glass partition; the measured clearance remains nominal until contact. Safety against such failures cannot come from statistical evaluation or software monitors alone. It requires physical zoning\index{Safety!physical zoning}, mechanical current limiters\index{Actuator!current limiters}, and independent physical safety barriers whose protective capability is validated independently of the learned model under specified physical assumptions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Physical failures undetectable by sensory telemetry are formally cataloged in @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors.
:::

These limits bind even a flawless campaign. The evidence that survives them is only as good as the campaign that produced it, and procedural and statistical errors can corrupt a campaign long before its result reaches the record.

## Empirical Evaluation Pitfalls and Metric Masking {#sec-evaluation-failure-modes}

Systematic errors undermining policy evaluation rarely stem from deliberate fraud. They arise when an evaluation protocol answers an easier question than the claim asks, creating statistical or procedural mirages that mask physical vulnerability.

### Six procedural evaluation pathologies {#sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies}

Six recurring procedural flaws distort empirical evaluation: environment selection, metric drift, test-set contamination, optional stopping, denominator filtering, and substituting demonstrations for measurements.

**Pathology 1: Environment selection.** Environment selection occurs whenever the test bench is narrower than the claim. The twenty door runs all met the nominal strike plate at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach with the base stopped and the tote rack empty. If the report states their success rate as the machine's ability to open the site's cage doors, the claim silently expands to the `{python} EvalMachine.n_absences_str` unsampled cells of the ledger and the loaded machine (@sec-evaluation-limits). Environment selection\index{Environment selection} is detected by comparing a condition ledger, which records the measured strike-plate position, approach speed, payload, and floor condition of every trial, against the boundaries of the claimed domain; a ledger that covers one cell establishes nothing about the others.

**Pathology 2: Metric drift and offline surrogate substitution.** Metric drift\index{Metric drift} occurs when the evaluation metric slides from physical closed-loop task completion toward an offline surrogate such as action agreement\index{Action agreement}, validation loss, action Mean Squared Error (MSE), or action cosine similarity against recorded expert buffers. Offline scoring is cheap, so the substitution happens gradually, and it inherits the ranking inversions of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics. Metric drift is prevented by mandating that the primary evaluation metrics remain closed-loop physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), with zero unmitigated tripwire crossings.

**Pathology 3: Unit-specific test set contamination.** Repeated tuning against a fixed evaluation setup creates **unit-specific test set contamination**\index{Test set contamination}. Adjusting the checkpoint or observation filtering after each batch on Unit 01 makes that robot and door part of development, not an independent holdout. The resulting improvement may depend on their particular backlash, calibration, and lighting. Audit the history of policy versions, tuning decisions, and chassis identities, and reserve fresh units and conditions for any claim that requires generalization beyond the development setup.

**Pathology 4: Optional stopping and multi-look inflation.** An engineer who watches a sequence of physical runs and halts as soon as the tally crosses a target reports a confidence the procedure does not have. Each look at the accumulating result is another chance for a false positive. `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_looks_str` independent 5 percent looks would have a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_any_false_positive_pct_str` percent chance of at least one false positive. Repeated looks at one accumulating run are dependent, so the inflation for a real stopping rule must be computed for that rule. Optional stopping\index{Optional stopping} cannot be detected from summary tables or final pass rates. It is detected only by auditing the pre-registered trial protocol, verifying that sample sizes, stopping conditions, and evaluation milestones were fixed before the first physical run began. The calibrated alternative is a sequential rule declared in advance (@sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt).

**Pathology 5: Denominator filtering and the censored trial fallacy.** A related distortion occurs when the denominator is quietly filtered, breaking the full-denominator condition of @sec-evaluation-trial-protocol. A team that discards runs ending on timeouts, emergency stops, sensor communication drops, or permission-path overrides as invalid test artifacts reports success over the surviving trials only. Every metric of @sec-evaluation-what-measured then moves in the flattering direction: ACR rises, MTBI grows, intervention density falls toward zero, and the reset time spent clearing a jammed gripper disappears from the budget. If the arm opens the door on nine of ten attempts and the tenth needs an operator takeover to stop the gripper wedging against the latch, removing that attempt raises the apparent success rate from 90 percent to 100 percent and reports an infinite MTBI for the batch. Infrastructure aborts, such as dropped wireless packets, stalled kernel threads, or bus brownouts, also stay in the denominator. A base that stalls in the aisle because an operating system thread locked has failed its mission, whichever subsystem caused it, and removing such aborts evaluates an abstraction rather than the deployed machine. When physical constraints or safety limits truncate a run before its time limit $T_{\max}$ expires, the trial stays in the ledger as not unassisted ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$), and for the unassisted-failure event it is right-censored rather than omitted. Reading survival on truncated trajectories as operational competence is the censored trial fallacy\index{Censored trial fallacy} of @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes. Denominator filtering\index{Denominator filtering} is detected by cross-referencing low-level actuator telemetry and permission-path logs against the trial ledger, confirming that every power-on cycle, autonomy engagement, and physical reset corresponds to a recorded outcome.

::: {#ws-evaluation-nhtsa-40-percent-mirage .callout-war-story title="The 2017 NHTSA Autopilot crash rate mirage"}
**Context**: In January 2017, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) closed Preliminary Evaluation PE 16-007, which it had opened after a fatal Florida crash of a Model S operating in Autopilot mode (@sec-perception-failure-modes) [@nhtsa2017pe16007]. The closing report compared airbag-deployment crash rates in the subject Tesla vehicles before and after Autosteer was installed and stated that "the Tesla vehicles crash rate dropped by almost 40 percent after Autosteer installation," from 1.3 to 0.8 crashes per million miles.

**Mechanism**: The rate divided airbag deployments by miles driven before and after installation, and the report's own footnote noted that the rates "are for all miles travelled before and after Autopilot installation and are not limited to actual Autopilot use." The denominator therefore never measured exposure to Autosteer itself, and it was incomplete as well. A replication by Quality Control Systems Corporation found that the odometer reading at installation appears to have been reported for fewer than half of the vehicles, and that exact exposure before and after installation could be computed for only 13 percent of them [@qcs2019nhtsa]. The mileage NHTSA left uncounted, because it could be assigned to neither period, was concentrated among the vehicles with the least exposure before installation.

**Impact**: In the one cohort with complete exposure in both periods, the airbag-deployment crash rate rose 59 percent after installation, from 0.76 to 1.21 per million miles, a result the replication qualified with "if these data are to be believed." Its authors concluded that the overall 40 percent reduction was "an artifact of the Agency's treatment of mileage information that is actually missing in the underlying dataset." The replication does not measure Autosteer's effect either. It shows that the published denominator could not support the reported reduction.

**Response**: The correction came from outside the agency and two years after the closing report, because the per-vehicle mileage records that exposed the denominator were released only after a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Transportation [@qcs2019nhtsa].

**Systems lesson**: In physical AI evaluation, an unverified denominator produces a statistical mirage. Aggregating open-world mileage without engagement telemetry, operational design domain boundaries, and complete exposure records turns missing data into a safety claim. An evaluation audits the integrity of its denominator with the same rigor it applies to the failure events in its numerator.
:::

**Pathology 6: Substituting visual demonstrations for statistical measurements.** A successful video shows that the machine reached the goal under one sequence of conditions; without a sampling record, it does not establish how often that outcome recurs. Smooth $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ kinematics (rigid-body motions in three dimensions)\index{SE(3) kinematics} can conceal small physical margins. A representative campaign needs predeclared sampling from the target ODD or separate per-stratum analysis, full-denominator accounting, and a sample size tied to its stated claim.

None of these pathologies is visible in the final pass rate. Each is caught only by auditing the record against the protocol that was declared before the first run, which is why the evaluation record keeps the protocol, the condition ledger, and the complete outcome sequence rather than the summary alone.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-evaluation-fallacies-pitfalls}

An evaluation supports claims only within its tested conditions and limits. These mistakes arise when teams extend a result beyond those limits or attribute an architectural safeguard to the learned policy.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Repeated success in a single nominal condition proves broad operational readiness.*

The door campaign repeats one condition twenty times: the nominal strike plate, the guarded approach, the base stopped, the rack empty. Under the binomial model\index{Evaluation!binomial model}, those runs give the `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent lower bound of \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} for that condition\index{Evaluation!confidence intervals}, and nothing for the other cells of the ledger or a loaded tote rack that moves the arm's torque margins. Repeating the condition sharpens the nominal estimate while the deployment-critical envelopes\index{Safety!operational envelope} stay untested. A readiness claim must name its target ODD, allocate trials across the physical variations inside it, and report uncertainty within each tested cell. **Nominal repetition sharpens precision on a single cell; it provides zero evidence for the rest of the operational design domain.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Explicitly partition the declared ODD into a condition matrix, allocate test quotas across all operational strata, and report confidence intervals per cell rather than pooling unstratified runs.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero failures in 1,000 trials proves compliance with a 99.9 percent reliability specification.*

Suppose the latch policy opens the door `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_fallacy_str` times without a trip against a requirement of 99.9 percent success at 95 percent confidence. The observed success fraction is perfect ($\hat{p} = 1.00$), and textbook Central Limit Theorem Wald intervals collapse into the degenerate point $[1.0, 1.0]$ because estimated variance $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n$ vanishes identically. Yet exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson inversion ($p_{\text{lower}} = 0.05^{1/n}$) demonstrates that the true one-sided lower confidence bound is only `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_fallacy_str`, falling short of the 99.9 percent requirement (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds); certifying it requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs. A parallel fallacy occurs in early-stage pilot evaluation: observing zero failures in 20 trials ($p_{\text{lower}} =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent) cannot demonstrate even a 90 percent success lower limit (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_90_str` clean runs required), let alone an industrial 99 percent limit (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_99_str` clean runs required). The trial budget follows strictly from the claim and confidence level, fixed in advance, and the report must state the exact Clopper-Pearson lower bound rather than the perfect empirical fraction. **Zero failures with an insufficient sample size represents an evidence deficit, not an empirical proof of compliance.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Reject asymptotic Wald intervals at parameter boundaries; precalculate the required sample size via the non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson bound ($n = \lceil \ln\alpha_{\text{sig}} / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$) or the Poisson Rule of Three ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), and report exact one-sided lower confidence bounds.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *High offline action agreement on static logs guarantees closed-loop physical stability.*

An evaluation report that cites close agreement with expert actions\index{Evaluation!action agreement} on recorded runs, such as negligible action MSE, high discrete token accuracy, low validation perplexity, or high action cosine similarity, has measured dataset imitation on frozen buffers and nothing more. The aisle policy of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics matched its recordings almost exactly and still spent its side clearance through the kinematic integration of a persistent heading bias. Covariate shift\index{Evaluation!covariate shift} adds a separate risk when the resulting states leave the demonstrations. Furthermore, at non-Lipschitz mechanical contact interfaces, sub-millimeter errors that barely register in MSE trigger destructive reaction forces ($F = k \Delta x$) and mechanical jamming, producing severe ranking inversions where low-MSE policies fail while higher-MSE policies succeed. Similarly, action cosine similarity discards command magnitude entirely; a policy that commands the right direction with 25 percent too little force stalls below the latch's release force, while one that commands 150 percent of the required force can cross the contact tripwire. Offline surrogates can screen candidate checkpoints before physical trials, but empirical closed-loop behavior must be characterized with physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) counted against the full denominator. These finite-sample metrics are not a closed-loop stability proof\index{Control!closed-loop stability}. **Offline validation loss, MSE, and cosine similarity measure dataset mimicry; closed-loop physical dynamics decide survival.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Treat offline loss, action MSE, and cosine similarity strictly as preliminary screening filters; require closed-loop physical rollouts with full-denominator accounting for a behavioral claim, and a separate model-based argument for any claimed stability guarantee.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Peeking at accumulating rollouts and terminating testing early inflates false safety certification.*

An engineering team halts after 30 clean runs because the accumulating result looks favorable, then reports the confidence of a fixed-sample test. That stopping rule changes the test; its error rate cannot be read from a fixed-sample calculation. A predeclared zero-failure protocol may stop at a failure to reject the candidate, but early acceptance needs its own calibration. Sequential probability ratio testing supplies one such approach: Ville's inequality bounds its false acceptance by $e^{-A}$ for whatever acceptance boundary $A$ the protocol declares, which is $\alpha_{\text{sig}}/(1-\beta)$ for Wald's boundary (@sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt). **Choose the stopping rule before collecting outcomes, and report the error guarantee for that rule.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Pre-register sequential decision boundaries ($A \approx \ln((1-\beta)/\alpha_{\text{sig}})$, $B \approx \ln(\beta/(1-\alpha_{\text{sig}}))$) and update the log-likelihood ratio $\Lambda_m$ after each rollout, halting testing only when it crosses a declared boundary.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Crediting the learned policy with surviving transport stalls that the enforcement architecture handled.*

The mobile manipulator completes 50 nominal aisle runs, and the team credits its learned policy with tolerance to SerDes bus jitter\index{Hardware!SerDes jitter}. A qualification test then injects a mailbox stall that outlasts the chosen `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences. The lease\index{Safety!freshness lease} expires, and the permission path detects the stale lease and initiates a controlled dynamic stop, analogous to a Category 1 stop\index{Safety!Category 1 stop}, from the fallback ladder of @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. That response comes from the enforcement architecture; nominal completion records do not establish that the neural weights detect or compensate for the stall. Fault injection\index{Evaluation!fault injection} must measure the permission path's detection and stopping behavior against the available stopping distance margin, and the evaluation report must attribute the protection to the hardware mechanism that supplied it. **Do not credit unverified neural weights with safety guarantees provided by the deterministic permission path.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Conduct systematic fault injection (injecting communication stalls and sensor dropouts) to independently benchmark the permission path's stopping envelope, and attribute safety mechanisms strictly to the hardware and software layers that executed them.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero physical collisions or hardware damage in testing proves high autonomous policy reliability.*

When an autonomous vehicle or mobile manipulator completes an extended campaign with zero collisions, teams frequently declare that the policy achieved high reliability (e.g., claiming an MTBF equal to total run time). But if human safety supervisors or runtime permission-path filters intervened repeatedly to prevent impending impacts, the system achieved zero hardware damage ($N_{\text{damage}} = 0$) only because the protective safety envelope intervened to censor the failure trajectories. What the testbed actually measured was an intervention event; the true autonomous reliability is captured by Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR) and Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI). Frequent human takeovers can make a proposed service impractical, while frequent automatic least-change adjustments may be normal operation; the report must separate those classes. Discarding these interventions or treating them as unassisted proposer successes confuses the protective competence of the safety architecture with the operational competence of the learned policy. **Zero collisions under active safety supervision must be interpreted alongside interventions; they do not by themselves establish policy reliability or complete protection coverage.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Enforce full-denominator accounting; record every supervisory takeover, permission-path clamping event, and tripwire crossing as an autonomy failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$), and report those strict autonomy measures beside whole-machine task completion, cycle time, and protective outcomes.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Qualifying a policy on a single reference robot assumes zero unit-to-unit hardware variance across the fleet.*

An engineering team executes 300 failure-free runs on a single robot (Unit 01) and declares the policy qualified for fleet release. When flashed onto Unit 02, the policy repeatedly jams or chatters. The unit-to-unit differences of @sec-evaluation-what-measured (transmission lost motion and stiffness, structural link compliance under load, camera bracket mounting, and stator winding tolerances) alter the plant transfer function across physical chassis. Testing on a single golden unit measures that individual unit's specific mechanical quirks, not fleet-wide reliability. Furthermore, testing at a single time of day ignores environmental unobservables, such as diurnal solar glare angling through clerestory windows, changing floor friction from ambient humidity, or motor winding heating ($I^2 R$), that shift physical dynamics without changing a single neural weight. **Evaluating a single robot chassis characterizes that specific unit's mechanical quirks; fleet release requires stratifying trials across the manufacturing distribution.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Stratify physical qualification across multiple chassis serial numbers drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, audit unit-specific lost motion and kinematic offsets, and quarantine final qualification testing to fresh units that were not used during policy development.

:::

## Summary {#sec-evaluation-summary}

Closed-loop evaluation measures the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol, so a success rate describes a declared population rather than a weight file. Because the machine's own admitted actions choose the states it reaches, which is Part II's endogenous-data principle, only trials that close the loop through the permission path measure what the proposer does; open-loop scores cannot see the drift those actions produce. A zero-failure confidence limit then bounds the sampled population under its sampling assumptions, and censoring at the edge of safe operation keeps that population inside the envelope the campaign could afford to enter. More trials narrow that bound without widening the population, and the exposure wall places rare-hazard rates beyond any campaign a physical machine can run.

The door campaign shows the shape of the claim that survives. Twenty clean runs support a lower confidence limit for the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, with the base stopped and unloaded, and nothing about the displaced-plate cells the demonstrations never covered or about the loaded machine. The coverage gap catalog records the conditions no trial visited, and assigns them to independent physical constraints and a feasible fallback on the permission path rather than to the proposer, because a runtime OOD detector can miss what it has never seen.

The stipulated recovery branch shows how this boundary can expand. Fresh experience supports a changed candidate, and independent nominal regression and displaced-plate qualification support the new record. The initial archive is not a permanent ceiling on future competence.

The chapter's product is the evaluation record, and four of its parts travel forward:

1. *Bounded operational claim:* The target ODD\index{Operational design domain!target ODD}, inside the policy manifest's declared ODD, where performance was empirically characterized.
2. *Reproducible configuration and ledger:* Digests of weights, firmware, and calibration, with unit-specific hardware tolerances and every attempted, aborted, and overridden trial kept in the denominator to derive honest physical metrics ($\text{ACR}$, MTBI, $D_{\text{int}}$, $T_{\text{reset}}$).
3. *Coverage gap catalog:* The known absences of the data and the manifest's omission log, plus the conditions and hardware units the trials left unvisited.
4. *Runtime monitor specifications:* For each boundary that can be sensed, the signal, threshold, and tested response that the permission path must implement at runtime\index{Runtime monitoring}.

@Tbl-07-key-equations collects the equations those claims rest on, each with the decision it supports.

| Equation                                                                                       | What it bounds or decides                                                                             | Derived in                                         |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| $p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$                       | The estimand: a success rate belongs to the declared population $\mathcal{D}$, not to the weights     | @eq-eval-estimand                                  |
| $t_{\text{impact}} = W_{\text{clear}}/(v \sin \epsilon_\theta)$                                | How soon a persistent heading bias spends clearance that open-loop scoring never sees                 | @eq-eval-clearance-time                            |
| $p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha_{\text{sig}}^{1/n}$                                                 | Success lower limit after $n$ clean trials                                                            | @eq-eval-zero-failure-bound                        |
| $p_{\text{fail, upper}} \approx 3/n$                                                           | Rule of Three: failure upper limit at 95% confidence, and $n \approx 3/(1-p_{\text{target}})$            | @eq-eval-rule-of-three                             |
| $n = \lceil \ln \alpha_{\text{sig}} / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$                            | Clean trials a claim needs; each added nine costs ten times the trials                                | @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size                  |
| $P(X \ge k \mid n, p) = \alpha_{\text{sig}}$                                                   | Success lower limit when the record contains failures                                                 | @eq-eval-bound-with-failures                       |
| $\Lambda_m$ against $A \approx \ln((1-\beta)/\alpha_{\text{sig}})$, $B \approx \ln(\beta/(1-\alpha_{\text{sig}}))$ | Sequential acceptance or rejection with both error rates declared before the first run | @eq-eval-sprt-llr and @eq-eval-sprt-boundaries     |
| $T \ge \ln(1/\alpha_{\text{sig}})/\lambda$                                                     | Exposure wall: failure-free hours before a hazard rate can be bounded                                 | @eq-eval-exposure-wall                             |
| $v_{\text{approach}} \le F_{\text{limit}}/\sqrt{m_{\text{red}}\, k_{\text{contact}}}$          | Precontact speed that keeps the first impact peak under a force limit                                 | @eq-eval-impact-speed                              |

: **Key equations of closed-loop evaluation**: Each equation fixes one quantity a campaign must declare or report. The statistical bounds assume independent, identically distributed draws from the declared population; the kinematic and contact relations are first-order models whose inputs must be measured on the machine. {#tbl-07-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Closed-loop evaluation and reliability"}
* **A success rate belongs to a population**: The rate reflects the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol. More runs tighten uncertainty within the sampled conditions; additional hardware units and operating conditions require evidence of their own.
* **Choose the regime for the question**: Replay screens prediction and computation, simulation probes modeled feedback, shadow operation measures execution on live inputs, and constrained physical trials expose real interaction. Each leaves a different gap; their results cannot be pooled as interchangeable trials.
* **Completion and intervention answer different questions**: ACR measures unassisted task completion, while MTBI and intervention density expose the burden of each declared intervention class. Whole-machine task completion and protective outcomes remain separate. Reset latency reveals the recovery cost. Retaining every attempted run prevents protection supplied by supervision from being credited to the policy.
* **Clean runs still leave uncertainty**: Twenty clean trials yield a one-sided 95 percent success lower limit of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent under iid sampling. The target and confidence determine the trial budget; predeclared, calibrated sequential rules can support early decisions without choosing a favorable stopping point afterward.
* **Rare hazards require independent protection evidence**: Feasible campaigns cannot supply arbitrary amounts of failure-free exposure. Runtime constraints and physical safeguards therefore need separate validation of their sensing, response, and fallback assumptions; a good policy score cannot supply that evidence.
* **The record carries capability and limits**: The evaluation record states what the proposer accomplished within its target ODD, preserves the complete ledger, and identifies unsupported conditions. Its monitor requirements guide runtime design, while unmonitorable gaps remain restrictions on the operational claim.
:::

The endogenous-data principle makes the evaluation record conditional. A run of incident-free trials samples the states the admitted actions reached; it neither covers every reachable state nor proves that hazards exist beyond the sample. The engineer must carry both the measured competence and the remaining uncertainty into runtime design. The evaluation record makes that handoff explicit through its target operating domain, coverage gaps, and monitoring requirements. Part III builds the sensing, state estimation, and permission mechanisms needed to act within those limits; their integrated verification follows before a release claim can rely on them.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-evaluation-history}

The statistics this chapter leans on were settled long before robots needed them. @wilson1927probable inverted the normal test so that an interval would not collapse at a perfect record, and @clopper1934use inverted the binomial tail itself to give the exact bound that a qualification record still reports. Clinical research supplied the shorthand. @hanley1983nothing named the rule of three for trials in which no patient suffered the adverse event, which is the question a clean robot campaign asks about its next run. Two-thirds of a century after the exact bound, @brown2001interval showed how poorly the textbook normal interval covers proportions near zero and one, the region where every qualification campaign lives.

The design of a campaign came from agriculture and from wartime. @fisher1935design built experiments around randomization and blocking so that uncontrolled variation could not pose as a treatment effect, and his exact test for small tables [@fisher1922interpretation] is the one a comparison of two latch checkpoints still uses. During the Second World War the Statistical Research Group at Columbia developed sequential testing to accept or reject production lots after fewer inspections, and @wald1945sequential published the method once its restriction lifted. The martingale argument that bounds its errors had already appeared in @ville1939etude, and it now underwrites the sequential comparisons of the robot-learning literature [@snyder2025policy].

The exposure wall entered engineering through avionics. @butler1993infeasibility showed that life testing cannot demonstrate the failure rates demanded of flight-critical software, and @kalra2016rr1478 carried the same arithmetic to road vehicles, counted in miles. The learning side began with imitation. @pomerleau1989alvinn steered a van by imitating a human driver, and the drift that follows when a cloned policy leaves the demonstrated states received its analysis two decades later [@ross2010efficient; @ross2011reduction], which made the gap between open-loop and closed-loop error a quantity with a bound. What this chapter adds is the record. A bounded claim states its population, keeps its interventions in the denominator, and hands the conditions it did not cover to the permission path.

For further reading, six works trace the lineage from small-sample statistics to robot evaluation practice.

- @brown2001interval compares the common intervals for a binomial proportion and shows where each fails. It is the reference behind the choice of the exact bound in @sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures.
- @wald1945sequential states the sequential probability ratio test with its boundaries and error bounds, in the form @sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt applies to the latch campaign.
- @butler1993infeasibility is short and still the clearest argument that testing alone cannot certify ultra-high reliability, and why the argument must shift to design.
- @kalra2016rr1478 works the exposure wall for road vehicles question by question, and its tables let a reader check every mileage requirement by hand.
- @ross2011reduction analyzes compounding error in imitation learning and gives the DAgger remedy, the formal account of why open-loop scores miss closed-loop failure.
- @kressgazit2024robot sets out reporting practices for physical policy evaluation, from run counts and initial conditions to blind trials and failure narratives, as a checklist a campaign can follow.

## Problems {#sec-evaluation-problems}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEM GIVENS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-problems.
# │ Goal:    Print each problem's givens from the registry and the chapter's
# │          cells, and guard the property each problem depends on, so a
# │          changed value cannot silently turn an intended answer around.
# │ Show:    givens only (answers live in the private instructor solutions):
# │          one-in-twenty policy; jammed-reset cycle; two failures; yaw-rate
# │          bias; chunk-miss targets; three-cell budget; four humanoid strata;
# │          shove-stratum success; the 300-run Unit 01 report.
# │ How:     Reuses EvalMachine, JamReset, DoorCycle, ClopperPearsonZeroFailure,
# │          BoundWithFailures (_cp_lower), Sprt, AisleDrift, and
# │          InterventionCampaign; zero-failure counts via
# │          calc_zero_failure_sample_size.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_time, fmt_percent, fmt_angle, check, MarkdownStr

class EvaluationProblems:
    """Givens for the Chapter 7 problems, with guards on the answers they imply."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_one_in_b = 20  # category: illustrative; a policy that fails one run in twenty (P1)
    n_fail_two = 2  # category: illustrative; failures in the two-failure campaign (P3)
    p_miss_a = 1e-6  # category: chosen; per-period chunk-miss target (P5)
    p_miss_b = 1e-9  # category: chosen; tighter per-period chunk-miss target (P5)
    yaw_bias = math.radians(0.5) * ureg.radian / ureg.second  # category: illustrative; persistent yaw-rate bias (P6)
    budget = 3000  # category: illustrative; affordable door trials (P8)
    n_cells_budget = 3  # category: illustrative; nominal, displaced plate, loaded rack (P8)
    n_strata = 4  # category: illustrative; humanoid disturbance strata (P10)
    p_strata_target = 0.90  # category: chosen; per-stratum success lower limit (P10)
    p_shove = 0.80  # category: illustrative; true success in the shove stratum (P10)
    n_unit01 = 300  # category: illustrative; clean runs in the Unit 01 report (P12)
    run_failed = 12  # category: illustrative; the failed run before the restart (P12)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha
    jam_cycle = (JamReset.t_run + JamReset.t_jam_reset).to(ureg.second)
    p_lower_two = _cp_lower(ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs - n_fail_two, ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs, alpha)
    n_restore = next(n for n in range(21, 200) if _cp_lower(n - 1, n, alpha) >= ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower)
    n_periods_a = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1 - p_miss_a, confidence=1 - alpha)
    t_hil_a = (n_periods_a * EvalMachine.chunk_period).to(ureg.hour)
    n_periods_b = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1 - p_miss_b, confidence=1 - alpha)
    t_hil_b = (n_periods_b * EvalMachine.chunk_period).to(ureg.year)
    t_yaw = ((2 * AisleDrift.clearance / (AisleDrift.v * yaw_bias.magnitude / ureg.second)) ** 0.5).to(ureg.second)
    per_cell = budget // n_cells_budget
    lo_marginal = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(per_cell, confidence=1 - alpha)
    lo_simultaneous = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(per_cell, confidence=1 - alpha / n_cells_budget)
    n_stratum = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_strata_target, confidence=1 - alpha / n_strata)
    p_shove_pass = p_shove**n_stratum
    lo_unit01 = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_unit01, confidence=1 - alpha)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check((1 - 1 / n_one_in_b) ** ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs > ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in, "P1: the one-in-twenty policy must log a clean record more often than the one-in-eight policy")
    check(abs(jam_cycle.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 85.0) < 1e-9, "P2: jammed-reset cycle should be 85 s")
    check(p_lower_two < BoundWithFailures.p_lower_one_fail, "P3: a second failure must lower the bound")
    check(n_restore == 33, "P3: restoring the clean twenty-run limit with one failure should need 33 runs")
    check(Sprt.B < Sprt.score_trace < Sprt.A, "P4: the trace must still be running after one failure")
    check(abs(t_hil_a.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 41.6) < 0.1, "P5: 1e-6 per period should need about 41.6 h of loaded execution")
    check(t_hil_b > 4 * ureg.year, "P5: 1e-9 per period must need years of loaded execution")
    check(t_yaw < AisleDrift.t_impact, "P6: the yaw-rate bias must spend the clearance sooner than the 1 degree heading offset")
    check(lo_simultaneous < lo_marginal < ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_target_999, "P8: splitting the budget must fall short of 99.9 percent per cell")
    check(calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(budget, confidence=1 - alpha) >= ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_target_999, "P8: the whole budget on one cell must reach 99.9 percent")
    check(n_stratum == 42 and p_shove_pass < 1e-3, "P10: 42 clean trials per stratum; the shove stratum almost never passes at 0.80")
    check(ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_target_99 < lo_unit01 < 0.991, "P12: 300 clean runs must just clear 99 percent on the tested cell")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_one_in_b_str = MarkdownStr({20: "twenty"}[n_one_in_b])
    jam_cycle_str = fmt_time(jam_cycle, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    n_fail_two_str = MarkdownStr({2: "two"}[n_fail_two])
    sprt_p0_str = fmt(Sprt.p0, precision=2)
    sprt_p1_str = fmt(Sprt.p1, precision=2)
    sprt_alpha_str = fmt(Sprt.alpha, precision=2)
    sprt_beta_str = fmt(Sprt.beta, precision=2)
    yaw_bias_str = fmt_angle(yaw_bias * ureg.second, unit=ureg.milliradian, precision=1)
    budget_str = fmt_int(budget, commas=True)
    budget_hours_str = fmt_time((budget * DoorCycle.t_cycle).to(ureg.hour), unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    n_strata_str = MarkdownStr({4: "four"}[n_strata])
    p_strata_target_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_strata_target, precision=0)
    p_shove_str = fmt(p_shove, precision=2)
    n_unit01_str = fmt_int(n_unit01)
    run_failed_str = fmt_int(run_failed)
```

Each problem states its givens, which come from the machine card (@tbl-01-machine-card), the aisle scenario behind it, or this chapter's calculations. A given marked illustrative is an assumption for the exercise, not a measurement. The tag names the kind of work, and the parenthesis names the learning objective the problem assesses.

1. **[Compute]** (Confidence bounds) The opening campaign logged `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` clean door runs. (a) Compute the probability of that record for a policy that fails one run in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_one_in_str` and for one that fails one run in `{python} EvaluationProblems.n_one_in_b_str` (both illustrative). (b) Find the success probability at which the record has probability $\alpha_{\text{sig}} =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str`, and check it against @eq-eval-zero-failure-bound. (c) In two sentences, state what the resulting 95 percent lower limit claims and what it does not, and decide whether the record excludes either policy.

2. **[Compute]** (Trial counts and test time) Using @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size, compute the clean door runs needed for success lower limits of 99 and 99.9 percent at 90, 95, and 99 percent confidence, and the test-cell hours each takes at the `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` door cycle. Repeat the hours for a cell in which every reset is the `{python} JamReset.t_jam_reset_str` jammed-latch reset of @sec-evaluation-what-measured, a `{python} EvaluationProblems.jam_cycle_str` cycle. Which lever, the confidence level or the target, costs more, and why?

3. **[Compute]** (Confidence bounds) A twenty-run campaign records `{python} EvaluationProblems.n_fail_two_str` failures (illustrative). Solve @eq-eval-bound-with-failures numerically for the 95 percent lower limit and compare it with the one-failure limit of `{python} BoundWithFailures.p_lower_one_fail_pct_str` percent and the clean limit of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent. Then find the smallest campaign with exactly one failure whose lower limit reaches the clean twenty-run limit. What does the answer imply for a team that plans twenty runs and hopes none will fail?

4. **[Compute]** (Stopping rules) Use the sequential test of @sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt with $p_0 =$ `{python} EvaluationProblems.sprt_p0_str`, $p_1 =$ `{python} EvaluationProblems.sprt_p1_str`, $\alpha_{\text{sig}} =$ `{python} EvaluationProblems.sprt_alpha_str`, and $\beta =$ `{python} EvaluationProblems.sprt_beta_str`. (a) From a score of zero, how many consecutive clean runs reach acceptance under @eq-eval-sprt-boundaries? (b) After `{python} Sprt.m_before_fail_str` clean runs and one failure, what is the score from @eq-eval-sprt-llr, and how many further clean runs reach acceptance? (c) A policy whose failure probability is exactly $p_1$ runs the fixed `{python} Sprt.n_fixed_90_str`-run zero-failure test instead. What is its probability of rejection, and to what does the sequential test bound that error? Decide which design you would register for a campaign whose runs wear a single unit.

5. **[Compute]** (Confidence bounds; evidence regimes) The latch policy must renew its chunk every `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str`, and a missed renewal leaves the active chunk running only until its `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` lease expires. How many consecutive on-time chunk periods bound the per-period miss probability at $10^{-6}$ with 95 percent confidence, and how many hours of loaded execution is that? Repeat for $10^{-9}$. Which evidence regime of @tbl-07-evidence-regimes can supply that exposure on the target silicon, which cannot, and what must carry the argument at $10^{-9}$?

6. **[Compute]** (Open-loop and closed-loop behavior) Unlike the fixed heading offset of @eq-eval-clearance-time, a candidate navigation policy carries a persistent yaw-rate bias of `{python} EvaluationProblems.yaw_bias_str` per second (illustrative). At the `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit, how long does the lateral drift take to spend the `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str` side clearance, and how far down the `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle does the base get? Compare with the $1.0^\circ$ heading case. Halve the speed and recompute both. Which bias does a speed restriction help more, in time and in distance, and why would an open-loop replay score miss the yaw-rate bias even more completely than the heading offset?

7. **[Compute]** (Completion and intervention metrics) An illustrative ten-run door ledger holds five clean runs; one run in which the permission path reduced the proposed force and the door opened on time; one tripwire stop with the door still latched; one operator takeover that freed a wedged gripper; one timeout with no intervention; and one bus-brownout abort that the drives' protective stop ended. Every run occupies `{python} JamReset.t_run_str` of active execution. The tripwire stop and the takeover each need the `{python} JamReset.t_jam_reset_str` jammed-latch reset, and every other run the `{python} DoorCycle.t_reset_str` nominal reset. Classify each run by $Y_i$, $A_i$, $I_i$, and protection outcome, then compute the task-completion rate, ACR, MTBI over all intervention classes, and the reset share of cell occupancy. Recompute after the team drops the takeover and the abort as "test artifacts," and state which conclusion changes.

8. **[Design]** (Trial protocol; conditional evidence) The facility can afford `{python} EvaluationProblems.budget_str` door trials (illustrative), `{python} EvaluationProblems.budget_hours_str` at the door cycle, to evaluate `latch-bc-recovery-02` across three cells: the nominal plate, the displaced plate, and the nominal plate with a loaded tote rack. Compare three allocations: every trial on the nominal cell; equal quotas with a marginal claim per cell; and equal quotas with $\alpha_{\text{sig}}$ split across cells for a simultaneous claim. For each, state the success lower limit each cell supports and the claim the record may make. Check each cell against the policy manifest's declared ODD, and propose the allocation you would predeclare.

9. **[Design]** (Evaluation record) Under the stipulated branch of @sec-evaluation-recovery-update, write the evaluation record for `latch-bc-recovery-02` in the fields of @tbl-07-evaluation-record-schema: its target ODD, the per-cell run counts for marginal and simultaneous 99.9 percent claims, its statistical evidence, a gap catalog, and two runtime monitor rows with signal, threshold, and tested response. One row covers chunk renewal against the `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period and `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` lease; the other covers latch contact force against the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` tripwire and the `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit. State one claim the record must refuse and the evidence that would be needed to make it.

10. **[Design]** (Rare failures; transfer to a humanoid) A humanoid's pick-and-place policy is to be qualified across `{python} EvaluationProblems.n_strata_str` disturbance strata fixed before collection: slippery floor, compliant floor, curb, and shove (illustrative). The claim is a `{python} EvaluationProblems.p_strata_target_pct_str` percent success lower limit in every stratum simultaneously at 95 percent confidence, and every failed trial is a fall. Compute the clean trials per stratum and in total. If the true success probability in the shove stratum is `{python} EvaluationProblems.p_shove_str` (illustrative), what is the chance that stratum passes, and how many falls would a campaign that ran all its trials expect there? Design the campaign: its stopping rule, its fall ledger, and which strata run free, tethered, or in simulation. Name the assumption of the door campaign that the humanoid breaks.

11. **[Critique]** (Completion and intervention metrics; rare failures) The supervised campaign of @sec-evaluation-limits, `{python} InterventionCampaign.n_int_str` interventions over `{python} InterventionCampaign.n_missions_str` missions with no damage, is written up as "MTBF of `{python} InterventionCampaign.t_active_str`, `{python} InterventionCampaign.d_int_str` interventions per kilometer, zero collisions: ready for unsupervised aisle operation." Compute the MTBI and the exact 95 percent interval on the intervention rate. Then state what the report can claim, what it cannot claim about MTBF, ACR, and safety, and which ledger fields it would need to compute ACR.

12. **[Critique]** (Hardware, environment, and stopping rules) A team reports: "Run `{python} EvaluationProblems.run_failed_str` failed, so we fixed the observation filter and restarted. The fixed policy then passed `{python} EvaluationProblems.n_unit01_str` consecutive runs on Unit 01, every morning for a week, so it meets 99 percent at 95 percent confidence for the fleet." Compute the lower limit that `{python} EvaluationProblems.n_unit01_str` clean runs support, and identify each departure from the protocol of @sec-evaluation-trial-protocol and the pathologies of @sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies. State the claim the evidence does support and the campaign a fleet claim would need.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From evaluation records to perception"}
Part II ends with a record that confines trust in the learned proposer to its target ODD and names the runtime monitors the rest of the machine must supply. Part III builds the runtime that meets those obligations. The first of them falls on perception, because an input-support monitor or a latency monitor can act only on observations that carry their capture time, their coordinate frame, and their uncertainty. @Sec-perception follows a measurement from the sensor to a spatial claim that the permission path can date, place, and bound before it permits motion.
